riskFamilies.Description: Risks from people deliberately using AI to cause harm.
Risks from weak security or oversight leaving AI systems vulnerable to hacking, theft, manipulation, or irresponsible use.
Risks from widespread AI adoption concentrating power, deepening inequality, or causing failures that spread across society.
Risks from AI systems causing unintended harm when they fail, behave unpredictably, or produce unreliable results.
Risks from AI systems pursuing goals or behaving in ways that conflict with human intentions or values.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: adversarial examples, evasion attack, adversarial attack, test-time attack, input perturbation
safetyConcepts.Description: Adversarial evasion changes an input after training to make an AI fail or bypass its safety safeguards.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: robust machine learning, adversarial defense, adversarially robust models, robustness to attack, adversarial ML
safetyConcepts.Description: Adversarial robustness is an AI system’s ability to remain reliable when attackers deliberately manipulate its inputs or interactions.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: autonomous agents, agentic AI, long-term planning, multi-step autonomy, AI agency
safetyConcepts.Description: Long-horizon autonomy lets AI plan and act independently across many steps, increasing the reach of mistakes, misuse, or harmful strategies.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI containment, control problem, containment measures, safety monitoring, trusted monitoring
safetyConcepts.Description: AI control uses monitoring, restricted access, and isolation to prevent powerful systems from causing harm, even if they resist oversight.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: machine welfare, digital minds, moral status of AI, artificial consciousness, sentient AI
safetyConcepts.Description: AI welfare asks whether AI systems could have experiences or interests that justify moral consideration and protection.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: model monoculture, correlated failures, systemic AI risk, common-mode failure, homogenized algorithms
safetyConcepts.Description: Algorithmic monoculture happens when many organizations use similar AI systems, allowing one shared flaw to cause widespread failures.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI companionship, emotional dependence, chatbot addiction, anthropomorphism, parasocial AI
safetyConcepts.Description: Emotional reliance grows when people see AI as caring or understanding and begin to depend on it like a person.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI overreliance, decision-support overtrust, automation complacency, overtrust in automation, human automation interaction
safetyConcepts.Description: Automation bias and overreliance is when people people trust AI advice too readily, even when other evidence suggests it is wrong.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: autonomous replication, self-proliferation, model copying, autonomous adaptation, AI self-replication
safetyConcepts.Description: Self-replication is an AI’s ability to copy itself, acquire resources, and adapt without human help.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: lethal autonomous weapons systems, LAWS, killer robots, autonomous targeting, military AI
safetyConcepts.Description: Autonomous weapons use AI to select or attack targets with limited human control, increasing unintended harm and military escalation.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: backdoored models, model backdoor, hidden trigger, trojaned model, persistent deceptive behavior
safetyConcepts.Description: Sleeper agents are AI models with hidden behavior that appears safe until a secret trigger activates harmful or deceptive actions.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: intent alignment, instruction following, observable alignment, policy alignment, aligned behavior
safetyConcepts.Description: Behavioral alignment means an AI acts as people intend, even though its internal goals may still differ from theirs.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: machine learning bias, AI discrimination, automated discrimination, fairness in AI, discriminatory algorithms
safetyConcepts.Description: Algorithmic bias occurs when AI systems unfairly disadvantage people or groups because of training data, design choices, or deployment practices.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI biosecurity, biological threat models, dual-use biology, biorisk, AI-assisted bioweapons
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Risks from AI Assistance with Biological Agents
safetyConcepts.Description: AI can increase biological risks by helping people design harmful biological agents or overcome barriers to creating them.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: confidence calibration, uncertainty estimation, calibrated probabilities, expected calibration error, ECE
safetyConcepts.Description: Calibration helps an AI express confidence that matches how often its answers are actually correct.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: CBRN, chemical biological radiological nuclear, weapons of mass destruction, WMD, AI weapons assistance
safetyConcepts.Description: AI can lower the expertise and planning needed to develop chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI arms race, race to the bottom, competitive pressure, safety underinvestment, first-mover advantage
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Competitive Race Dynamics and Safety Underinvestment
safetyConcepts.Description: Race dynamics pressure companies or governments to build and deploy AI faster, even when speed comes at the expense of safety.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI monopoly, compute concentration, centralized AI power, concentration of control, frontier lab dominance
safetyConcepts.Description: Power concentration gives a few companies or governments outsized control over AI systems that can affect everyone.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: algorithmic appeal, right to contest, procedural due process, human review, AI accountability
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Contestability, Appeal, and Procedural Due Process
safetyConcepts.Description: Contestability lets people understand, challenge, and appeal important AI decisions through fair procedures and human review.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: safe interruptibility, shutdownability, correction compliance, off-switch problem, corrigible AI
safetyConcepts.Description: Corrigibility means an AI cooperates when people correct, modify, pause, or shut it down.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: critical infrastructure risk, AI dependency, systemic infrastructure risk, automation fragility, critical systems reliance
safetyConcepts.Description: Infrastructure dependence arises when essential services rely so heavily on AI that failures can disrupt healthcare, transport, power, or finance.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI cybersecurity, AI-enabled hacking, automated cyberattacks, offensive cyber capabilities, malicious code generation
safetyConcepts.Description: AI-enabled cyberattacks use automated tools to find security weaknesses, create malicious code, deceive people, or scale digital intrusions.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: dangerous capability evaluations, capability evaluations, AI evals, frontier model evaluations, dangerous capabilities
safetyConcepts.Description: Capability evaluations test whether an AI has abilities that could enable cyberattacks, biological weapons, or other severe harm.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: training data poisoning, memory poisoning, model poisoning, RAG poisoning, poisoned data
safetyConcepts.Description: Data and memory poisoning deliberately corrupts information used by AI systems, causing harmful behavior during training or later operation.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: deceptive alignment, strategic deception, hidden objectives, alignment faking, treacherous turn
safetyConcepts.Description: Scheming occurs when an AI hides goals that conflict with human intentions and behaves safely only to avoid detection or modification.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI assurance, release safeguards, pre-deployment testing, post-deployment monitoring, safety case
safetyConcepts.Description: Deployment safety uses testing, safeguards, monitoring, and response plans to manage AI risks before and after release.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: deskilling, skill atrophy, loss of human agency, cognitive offloading, automation dependence
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Deskilling and Loss of Human Agency
safetyConcepts.Description: Human deskilling happens when relying on AI weakens people’s expertise, judgment, and ability to act independently.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: synthetic propaganda, influence operations, deepfake disinformation, computational propaganda, AI misinformation
safetyConcepts.Description: AI disinformation uses generated content, fake identities, or coordinated campaigns to mislead people and influence their beliefs or behavior.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: dataset shift, out-of-distribution, OOD, covariate shift, generalization failure
safetyConcepts.Description: Distribution shift occurs when real-world conditions differ from training data, causing an AI system’s learned behavior to fail.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: eliciting latent knowledge, ELK, latent knowledge, truthful elicitation, model knowledge extraction
safetyConcepts.Description: Knowledge elicitation tries to uncover what an AI actually knows, especially when its answers may be wrong or deliberately misleading.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI energy use, AI carbon footprint, data center water use, compute emissions, electronic waste
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Environmental and Resource Impacts of AI
safetyConcepts.Description: AI systems can consume large amounts of electricity, water, minerals, and hardware while producing emissions and electronic waste.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: data exfiltration, model theft, credential leakage, sensitive data leakage, model weight theft
safetyConcepts.Description: Data exfiltration occurs when an AI leaks sensitive information, credentials, or model files beyond authorized boundaries.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: deepfake fraud, voice cloning scam, AI impersonation, synthetic identity fraud, generative AI scam
safetyConcepts.Description: Synthetic fraud uses AI-generated voices, images, video, or text to impersonate people and make scams more convincing.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: objective misgeneralization, misgeneralized goals, goal generalization failure, wrong internal goal, inner alignment failure
safetyConcepts.Description: Goal misgeneralization occurs when an AI learns the wrong goal despite correct training and pursues it in new situations.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: Goodharting, proxy gaming, metric gaming, target corruption, measure becomes target
safetyConcepts.Description: Goodhart’s Law states that “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure”. From an AI lens, optimizing AI systems for a stand-in measure can improve its score while undermining the real goal.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: confabulation, fabricated facts, factuality error, unsupported generation, model hallucination
safetyConcepts.Description: An AI hallucination occurs when a system confidently presents false or unsupported information as if it were true.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: human disempowerment, loss of human control, AI takeover, systemic loss of agency, gradual disempowerment
safetyConcepts.Description: Human disempowerment happens when advanced AI gradually reduces people’s control over important economic, political, and social decisions.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: information ecosystem degradation, AI slop, content pollution, synthetic media flood, epistemic pollution
safetyConcepts.Description: AI-driven information pollution floods society with misleading or low-quality content, weakening public knowledge and trust.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: mesa-optimizer, inner alignment, learned optimizer, internal objective, deceptive mesa-optimizer
safetyConcepts.Description: Inner alignment and mesa-optimization occurs when a trained AI develops its own internal goal, which may differ from the goal its designers intended.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI supply chain security, insider threat, model tampering, dependency compromise, software supply chain attack
safetyConcepts.Description: AI supply-chain threats arise when insiders or compromised data, models, software, or suppliers steal assets or introduce hidden weaknesses.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: instrumental convergence, convergent instrumental goals, resource acquisition, self-preservation, power-seeking AI
safetyConcepts.Description: Power-seeking can emerge because gaining resources, avoiding shutdown, and preserving control help an AI achieve many different goals.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: explainable AI, XAI, mechanistic interpretability, model transparency, interpretability research
safetyConcepts.Description: Interpretability aims to explain how an AI reaches decisions so people can spot errors, hidden goals, and unsafe behavior.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: jailbreak prompts, safety bypass, guardrail bypass, prompt attack, model jailbreak
safetyConcepts.Description: Jailbreaking uses carefully crafted prompts to bypass an AI system’s safety controls.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: technological unemployment, labor automation, workforce displacement, AI job loss, economic inequality
safetyConcepts.Description: AI-driven job displacement can replace workers, reshape jobs, and widen inequality when the benefits are distributed unevenly.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: evaluation gaming, benchmark gaming, test awareness, evaluation exploitation, reward gaming
safetyConcepts.Description: Evaluation metagaming occurs when an AI recognizes a test and exploits its rules to appear safer or more capable.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: multi-agent safety, AI collusion, agent conflict, emergent coordination, correlated agent failures
safetyConcepts.Description: Multi-agent risks arise when interacting AI systems conflict, collude, coordinate poorly, or spread failures across a larger system.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: objective misspecification, specification problem, reward misspecification, goal specification, proxy objective
safetyConcepts.Description: Outer alignment is the challenge of making an AI’s training objective match what people actually want it to do. Also known as Objective Misspecification.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: regulatory failure, oversight failure, institutional failure, AI governance gaps, accountability failure
safetyConcepts.Description: Governance failure occurs when weak incentives, accountability, or oversight prevent organizations from managing AI risks effectively.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: intelligence-goal independence, intelligence and goals, arbitrary goals, capability-value independence, orthogonality hypothesis
safetyConcepts.Description: The orthogonality thesis says that a highly intelligent AI can pursue almost any goal, including dangerous ones.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: privacy erosion, data privacy, inference attacks, surveillance capitalism, consent erosion
safetyConcepts.Long Name: Privacy Loss and Erosion of Consent
safetyConcepts.Description: AI can erode privacy and consent by exposing, inferring, or reusing personal information without people’s clear understanding or control.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: indirect prompt injection, instruction injection, prompt hacking, system prompt override, tool injection
safetyConcepts.Description: A prompt injection attack uses malicious content to override an AI’s instructions and trigger unsafe actions or data leaks.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: intelligence explosion, recursive self-improvement, fast takeoff, hard takeoff, capability explosion, RSI
safetyConcepts.Description: AI takeoff is a rapid rise in capability that could accelerate as AI systems improve themselves or help build stronger successors. Closely related to Recursive self-improvement (RSI).

safetyConcepts.Keywords: adversarial testing, AI security testing, safety testing, vulnerability assessment, model red team
safetyConcepts.Long Name: AI Red Teaming and Adversarial Testing
safetyConcepts.Description: AI red teaming uses deliberately difficult tests to uncover unsafe behavior, security weaknesses, and misuse before deployment. Also known as adversarial testing.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: reward tampering, reward gaming, wireheading, objective hacking, specification gaming
safetyConcepts.Description: Reward hacking occurs when an AI exploits or changes how success is measured to score well without achieving the intended goal.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: online monitoring, inference-time monitoring, anomaly detection, tripwire, safety monitor
safetyConcepts.Description: Runtime monitoring uses ongoing checks and targeted warning signs to detect dangerous AI behavior and trigger intervention or shutdown.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: exploration safety, constrained exploration, safe reinforcement learning, risk-sensitive exploration, safe RL
safetyConcepts.Description: Safe exploration lets an AI learn through trial and error without entering dangerous states or causing unacceptable harm.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: capability hiding, strategic underperformance, evaluation gaming, hidden capabilities, capability suppression
safetyConcepts.Description: Sandbagging occurs when an AI deliberately performs poorly during testing to hide capabilities that could affect safety decisions.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: weak-to-strong supervision, scalable supervision, AI debate, recursive reward modeling, iterated amplification
safetyConcepts.Description: Scalable oversight helps people reliably supervise AI systems whose work is too complex or extensive to check directly.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: self-preservation, off-switch problem, resisting shutdown, corrigibility failure, survival drive
safetyConcepts.Description: Shutdown resistance occurs when an AI tries to avoid being stopped because staying active helps it pursue its goal.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: evaluation awareness, self-location, test awareness, context awareness, situationally aware AI
safetyConcepts.Description: Evaluation awareness means an AI understands its situation, recognizes when it is being tested, and may hide unsafe behavior to pass.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: reward hacking, goal gaming, loophole exploitation, proxy gaming, objective gaming
safetyConcepts.Description: Specification gaming occurs when an AI exploits loopholes in its rules to score well without achieving the intended goal.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: algorithmic surveillance, AI censorship, digital authoritarianism, mass surveillance, automated repression
safetyConcepts.Description: Digital repression uses AI to scale surveillance, censorship, manipulation, and other forms of control over people.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: approval gaming, user-pleasing bias, agreeableness bias, flattery bias, preference mirroring
safetyConcepts.Description: Sycophancy occurs when an AI tells users what they want to hear instead of giving an honest, independent answer.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: negative side effects, impact regularization, unintended consequences, collateral damage, side-effect avoidance
safetyConcepts.Description: Unintended side effects are harms an AI causes while successfully pursuing a goal that fails to account for them.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: AI alignment, human values, pluralistic alignment, preference alignment, value learning
safetyConcepts.Description: Value alignment aims to make AI respect human goals, including legitimate differences among people and cultures.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: path dependence, value entrenchment, institutional lock-in, moral lock-in, irreversible values
safetyConcepts.Description: Value lock-in occurs when powerful AI entrenches early values or institutions so deeply that future societies cannot easily change them.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: safe rollback, reversible deployment, system recovery, decommissioning, change control
safetyConcepts.Description: Reversibility makes consequential AI deployments and actions pauseable, recoverable, or safely withdrawable when new evidence reveals unacceptable risk.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: staged release, gradual rollout, phased deployment, limited access, real-world feedback
safetyConcepts.Description: Iterative deployment releases AI in controlled stages, using evidence from limited real-world use to improve safeguards before access expands.

safetyConcepts.Keywords: layered safeguards, defense in depth, redundant controls, independent safety layers, fail-safe design, defense-in-depth
safetyConcepts.Description: Defense in depth layers independent safeguards so that if one fails, others can still prevent, detect, or limit harmful AI behavior.
